open_questions.q: Exactly which jobs does anthocyanin do for each plant: shading the leaf, coping with cold, calling insects, or others?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found evidence for several jobs. Which one matters most seems to differ from plant to plant, and scientists are still testing the ideas.

open_questions.q: How does a sour taste cell on the tongue sense acid?
open_questions.why_open: In 2019, scientists found a channel in sour taste cells that lets hydrogen particles in. They are still working out how this and other parts together give us the feeling of sourness.

open_questions.q: How fast, and how much, will the sea's pH keep changing as carbon dioxide rises?
open_questions.why_open: The sea is slowly becoming less basic. How fast this goes, and how it will affect corals and shellfish, depends on what people do with carbon dioxide.

jokes.j: Why did the cabbage water blush?
What did the purple cabbage water say to the soap?
jokes.a: You make me green with envy.

jokes.j: Why did the lemon go to the doctor?
Why was the vinegar so good at arguing?
jokes.a: It always had a sharp answer.

jokes.j: Knock knock. Who's there? Lemon. Lemon who?
jokes.a: Lemon in, it's cold out here!

jokes.j: What do you call a soap that tells jokes?
Why did the curd win the prize?
jokes.a: It was the most cultured one there.

maths.problem: Lakshmi, the girl in the story, tested five liquids. On the pH scale they are: lemon juice 2, buttermilk 5, water 7, cooking soda water 8, detergent water 11. Put them in order from the most basic to the most acidic. Which liquid is furthest from water?
maths.answer: Detergent water 11, cooking soda water 8, water 7, buttermilk 5, lemon juice 2. Lemon juice is furthest from water.
maths.explain: The biggest number is the most basic, so we start at 11 and go down. Lemon juice is 7 minus 2, which is 5 steps from water. Detergent water is 11 minus 7, which is 4 steps from water. 5 is more than 4, so lemon juice is furthest.
maths.context: This is about ordering the liquids from the Cabbage Colour Line test by their pH numbers.
maths.why_maths: Ordering numbers is how we turn a row of colours into a line we can compare exactly.

maths.problem: In the Lemon or Buttermilk test, Divya, a girl in Class 3, did the Lemon or Buttermilk test. Her lemon glass needed 6 spoons of soda water to turn purple. Her buttermilk glass needed 2 spoons. How many times as many spoons did the lemon glass need? How many spoons would 2 teaspoons of lemon juice need?
maths.answer: 3 times as many. 2 teaspoons of lemon juice would need about 12 spoons.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 2 is 3, so the lemon glass needed 3 times as many spoons. One teaspoon of lemon needed 6 spoons. Twice as much lemon has twice as much acid, so it needs 2 lots of 6, which is 12 spoons.
maths.context: This is about the Lemon or Buttermilk test, where you counted spoons of soda water.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the counts tells us how much more acid one liquid has than the other, and lets us predict before we test.

maths.problem: Lakshmi, the girl in the story, set katori A at 8 in the morning on Monday. She set katori B at 8 in the morning on Tuesday. She tested both at 8 in the evening on Tuesday. How long had each katori been setting?
maths.answer: Katori B had 12 hours. Katori A had 36 hours.
maths.explain: From 8 in the morning to 8 in the evening is 12 hours, so katori B had 12 hours. Katori A started a whole day earlier, which adds 24 hours. 24 plus 12 is 36 hours.
maths.context: This is about the Milk to Curd test, where two katoris of curd were set on different days.
maths.why_maths: Working out how long each curd sat lets us connect the colour to the time the bacteria had to make acid.

maths.problem: In Back to Purple, your token is on square 12 and square 7 is purple. A lemon juice card moves you 2 squares towards pink. Can you land exactly on square 7 using lemon cards alone? Which kind of card would you need as well?
maths.answer: No. Lemon cards take you from 12 to 10, 8, then 6. You need a 1-square card, such as buttermilk or a big jug of plain water.
maths.explain: From 12, each lemon card takes away 2: 12, 10, 8, 6. You jump over 7, because 12 minus 7 is 5, and steps of 2 never add up to an odd number like 5. A 1-square card changes odd to even, so it lets you land on 7.
maths.context: This is about the Back to Purple board game.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the odd and even pattern tells you which cards can get you home before you draw them.

roots.context: We have tested sour and soapy liquids and lined them up by colour. Now we ask what the colour line tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Cabbage water turned pink in lemon juice, purple in plain water and green in detergent water. Buttermilk, soda and soap gave the colours in between. So sour and soapy are two ends of one line. The colour shows where each liquid sits.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into two boxes, acid or base, as if there were nothing between them. The many in-between colours show a smooth line, and neutral water is just one place on it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Cabbage Colour Line, every liquid found its own place between pink and green. In Lemon or Buttermilk, spoon by spoon of soda water moved the same glass along the line from pink to purple to blue.

three.who_am_i: Your tongue can taste where a food sits on the line. Sour foods are near the acid end. Your blood stays at almost the same place on the line all your life.
three.what_is_life: Curd bacteria make milk sour to keep the milk for themselves. Weaver ants squirt acid to guard their nests. Living beings use acids to live.
three.what_is_this_world: Rain is a little acidic and the sea is a little basic. Every pond, river and soil has its own place on the line.

roots.thread: Even plain water holds a tiny number of acid particles and base particles. In pure water there are exactly as many of each, so they balance. An acid tips the balance one way. A base tips it the other way. One balance, tipped by different amounts, gives every liquid its place, from lemon to soap. All the colours on your windowsill came from that one balance and one pigment.

teachings.teaching: In this chapter of the old Ayurveda book, sages argue about how many tastes there are. They agree on six: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. The Sanskrit word for sour is amla.
teachings.link: Long before chemistry, people knew sour was its own taste. The Latin word acidus also means sour, and that is where the word acid comes from. Bases often taste bitter, another of the six. Your tongue was the first indicator.

teachings.link: Spoons of lemon move cabbage water towards pink. Spoons of soda move it towards green. It is the same line, travelled in two directions.

science.text: Water always splits a tiny bit into charged hydrogen particles and charged particles of oxygen and hydrogen. In pure water there are equal numbers of each, which is why pure water is neutral at pH 7.
The pH of the sea has been falling slowly, from about 8.2 to about 8.1, because the sea takes in carbon dioxide that people add to the air.

other_view.view: The pH line is a useful tool that people made, and each liquid's number is just a count of charged particles. Linking it to a taste teaching from Ayurveda or a Greek saying is a nice picture, but it adds nothing to the chemistry.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat. Choices made: red cabbage water is made in the mixie with cold water, so no stove is needed. Clear glasses or white cups on white paper are asked for, because steel tumblers hide the colour. Every glass has a plain water control, because some city tap water makes cabbage water a little bluish. Only weak, food-safe acids and bases are tested. Detergent is made up by a grown-up. Toilet cleaners, drain cleaners and chuna appear only as 'grown-ups only' examples. The curd test needs two days because one katori must be set a day later. Its colour differences are gentle, so the steps say to compare side by side and accept 'the same' as a real result. Butterfly pea flowers are given as the alternative if no red cabbage can be found. The curd test now says when to make the cabbage water, and tells the family what to write if the second katori has not set.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1675, a French chemist called Nicolas Lémery wrote a chemistry book in Paris, the Cours de Chymie. It became one of the most read chemistry books of its time. Lémery wanted to explain why acids taste sour and sting the tongue. He said that the particles of an acid have sharp points, like tiny spikes, and they prick the tongue. He said that bases, which he called alkalis, have particles full of holes. When an acid meets an alkali, the spikes push into the holes and break off, and that makes the fizzing. After that, the mixture is neither sour nor soapy. It was a clever picture, but no one could see the spikes or test them. Over the next 200 years, chemists studied many acids. They found that every acid contains hydrogen. In 1884, a young Swedish chemist, Svante Arrhenius, explained that in water an acid gives out tiny charged particles of hydrogen. A base gives out other charged particles, made of oxygen and hydrogen together. When an acid and a base meet, these two kinds join and make water. That is why they use each other up. No spikes were needed.
how_we_found_out.who: Nicolas Lémery, a French chemist in Paris, and later Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish chemist
how_we_found_out.when: 1675 (Lémery's Cours de Chymie) and 1884 (Arrhenius's work on charged particles in water)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Lémery thought acids taste sour because their particles have sharp spikes, and that acids and alkalis fizz because the spikes break in the alkali's holes. Chemists found instead that all acids contain hydrogen, and Arrhenius showed that acids give out charged hydrogen particles in water, which join with a base's particles to make water.
